title: Abbe diffraction limit
references: Abbe, E., Beitraege zur Theorie des Mikroskops und der mikroskopischen Wahrnehmung, Archiv fuer mikroskopische Anatomie 9(1), 413-468 (1873), doi:10.1007/BF02956173
Born, M. and Wolf, E., Principles of Optics, 7th ed., Cambridge University Press (1999)

Hell, S. W. and Wichmann, J., Breaking the diffraction resolution limit by stimulated emission: stimulated-emission-depletion fluorescence microscopy, Optics Letters 19(11), 780-782 (1994), doi:10.1364/OL.19.000780
validity_domain: Smallest resolvable period d = lambda / (2 NA) of a far-field optical microscope with a lens of numerical aperture NA, at vacuum wavelength lambda, with conventional (linear, non-saturated) imaging.
limitations: Assumption imaging_method: under conventional_far_field the bound is lambda / (2 NA); under super_resolution (STED, localisation microscopy, structured illumination, near-field) this law gives no bound (0), so a smaller size is not inconsistent with it. Unstated, the engine answers CONDITIONAL: possible only with super-resolution techniques.
Far-field imaging with linear optics; near-field microscopy, STED, localisation microscopy (PALM, STORM) and structured illumination beat it, because they do not satisfy these assumptions
A claim of localisation precision of a single emitter is not a resolution in this sense
aperture is the numerical aperture NA = n sin(theta) of the objective, wavelength is the vacuum wavelength
Defined for a positive numerical aperture; the core checks no condition on it here
A lower bound on the resolvable distance: real instruments resolve a larger distance
